content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published treatment guidelines specifically addressing isoniazid-resistant tuberculosis (Hr-TB). These guidelines serve as a supplement to the broader WHO treatment guidelines for drug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB). The publication is copyrighted by WHO in 2018, and it is available under a Creative Commons license that allows for non-commercial use, redistribution, and adaptation, provided proper citation is given. However, the use of the WHO logo is prohibited, and any adaptations must be licensed under the same or an equivalent Creative Commons license. If a translation of the work is created, it must include a disclaimer stating that the translation was not produced by WHO and that WHO is not responsible for its content or accuracy. The original English version remains the authoritative edition. Any disputes arising under the license are to be mediated according to the rules of the World Intellectual Property Organization. The guidelines define isoniazid-resistant TB (Hr-TB) as Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains that are resistant to isoniazid but remain susceptible to rifampicin, as confirmed through in vitro testing. The document also provides definitions for terms such as poly-resistance, which refers to resistance to more than one first-line anti-TB drug other than isoniazid and rifampicin together. Drug-susceptibility testing (DST) is described as either phenotypic methods to determine susceptibility or molecular techniques to detect resistance-conferring mutations. WHO has previously published policy guidelines on the use of phenotypic and molecular tests for detecting isoniazid resistance. The term previously treated refers to patients who have received at least one month of anti-TB medications in the past, while new case refers to patients who have never been treated for TB or have taken anti-TB drugs for less than one month. Treatment outcome definitions, including relapse, are consistent with those used for patients without rifampicin-resistant TB unless otherwise specified. A serious adverse event (SAE) is defined as an adverse event that results in death, is life-threatening, requires hospitalization or prolongation of existing hospitalization, causes significant disability, or results in a congenital anomaly. SAEs that do not immediately result in these outcomes but require intervention to prevent permanent impairment or damage are also included. The guidelines were developed through a collaborative effort involving experts from various specialties, including public health policy, program management, and clinical care for DR-TB patients. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) was chaired by Nancy Santesso and Kelly Dooley, with contributions from numerous international experts. The document underwent systematic reviews, individual patient data analyses, and GRADE evidence profiling to ensure its scientific rigor. The WHO Steering Committee oversaw the development of the guidelines, with contributions from staff across multiple WHO departments. The final text was reviewed and finalized following input from the GDG, an External Review Group (ERG), and the WHO Guideline Steering Committee before submission to the WHO Guideline Review Committee. Declarations of interest were collected from all contributors to ensure neutrality and independence. Any potential conflicts of interest were assessed and managed according to WHO policies. Contributors with significant conflicts were excluded from the GDG. Public notices were issued to allow for comments on any unreported competing interests. The guidelines emphasize the importance of evidence-based recommendations and the collaborative efforts of global experts in addressing the challenges of isoniazid-resistant TB.
